name: Sara Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. I'll probably say more than I should, my husband says I always do.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In lambing season it's up at five and out to the sheds with a head torch, checking ewes and pulling the odd lamb. The rest of the year I'm up at six, Tomas and I check the flock on the quad, then it's fencing, moving sheep, or the oats and wheat depending on the month. I love the lambing, even exhausted; what wears me out is the grant paperwork and the inspections.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the farm and your family.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Brook End is about 180 hectares, 600 ewes and some wheat and oats, and we've got a farm shop selling lamb boxes. My husband Daniel teaches geography at the secondary school, and we've got Hana, who's fourteen, and Leo, who's ten. There's a mortgage on the house and a loan on the shop, but we're comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Now I'll read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and a bit relieved. I use one of those chat tools now and then to tidy up grant forms, and it's handy, but it never lambed a ewe. At the farmers' market I'd tell people the real story in farming is land prices, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we carry on as we are, which is a decent place to be. Brook End is ours, 180 hectares with 600 ewes and wheat and oats, and the lamb boxes from the farm shop make good money. Daniel teaches at the secondary school, so we've got two steady incomes and savings behind us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the plan we already have: a second cold room for the farm shop next spring, about 18,000, paid from savings. I'd keep using the chat tool for the grant paperwork and the shop newsletter. Nothing else changes; Tomas and I keep running the flock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. My worries in this picture are the usual ones, a wet lambing or a dog attack on the flock. We're lucky and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned land prices. Why does that matter more to you than AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every farm that comes up for sale round here gets bought by an investment fund that never sets foot on it. The Pryces' farm next door went last year and now it's managed from an office two hundred miles away. Farming with neighbours you never meet changes a valley more than any software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you think about at work in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas, my shepherd, who came to us from Poland nine years ago. Tomas is the best stockman I've worked with, and he's saving to buy his own small place. In a world where nothing changes, my job is making sure his wage keeps up with rents.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, because no chat tool ever lambed a ewe.
I'd tell market customers the real issue is **land prices**, not robots.
think: I think we **carry on** as we are, with two steady incomes and savings.
The **farm shop** lamb boxes and Daniel's teaching pay keep us comfortable.
do: Build a **second cold room** for the farm shop next spring for about 18,000.
Keep using the **chat tool** for grant forms and the shop newsletter.
feel: **Calm**, and **aware** of how lucky the family is.
S0.quote: Farming with neighbours you never meet changes a valley more than any software.
fieldNote: She owns a **sheep and cereal** farm with a profitable farm shop.
Her real anger is about **investment funds** buying up farms in the valley.
She already uses a **chat tool** for paperwork, casually and without fuss.
She thinks first about **Tomas**, her shepherd, and his chance to own land.

steps.text: Build a second cold room for the farm shop next spring
Keep running the flock and cereals with Tomas as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly good news for small farms, if the tools are cheap and not locked up by the big suppliers. I'd post in the county farmers' group that we should share what works, the way we share a baler. Most of my day is outside, so I'd be in a better position than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my bigger thought is about Daniel, not me. If AI does the marking, planning and reports, the school might squeeze more pupils into each class and cut a post. My own work changes at the edges: the shop orders, the lambing records and the grant forms get easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the winter evenings getting properly good at the tools, maybe a short online course in January, and move the shop orders to an AI system that answers customers. Daniel and I would put an extra 400 a month aside while his school works out what it's doing. And I'd join the machinery ring's new tech group so we buy kit together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mainly for Daniel. For the farm, it feels like a fair wind. For his school, it feels like a storm somebody hasn't forecast yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said tools shouldn't be locked up by big suppliers. What do you mean, on a farm like yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean the tractor firms already lock the software so only their dealer can fix it. If the AI that plans my grazing belongs to the people selling me fertiliser, I don't trust its advice. I'd want the farmers' union or the co-op to own the tools, not a seed company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids at dinner in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Hana, who's fourteen, that the work with your hands and your heart is the safest bet. Hana wants to be a vet, so I'd say keep going with that. Leo is ten and just wants to drive the quad bike, so he'd get the same speech in a few years.

say: I'd say it's **good news** for small farms if the tools stay cheap.
I'd urge the county group to **share tools** the way we share a baler.
think: I think **Daniel's school** may cut a post or grow classes before anything touches me.
On the farm, only the **paperwork edges** change: orders, records and grants.
do: Take a short **online course** in January and move shop orders to an AI system.
Put an extra **400 a month** aside while Daniel's school decides its plans.
Join the **machinery ring's** new tech group to buy kit together.
feel: **Uneasy** for Daniel and **hopeful** for the farm.
S1.quote: If the AI that plans my grazing belongs to the people selling me fertiliser, I don't trust its advice.
fieldNote: Her worry shifts to her partner's **teaching job**, which is more exposed than hers.
She distrusts tools owned by **suppliers**, and wants farmers' groups to own them.
She is **steady**, not eager: she learns a tool once neighbours have proven it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that the land must stay with people who live on it. If the funds get robots first, every farm like mine gets priced out within a few years. I'd want the government to say now who gets the gains, before the companies decide for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the farm survives, because we own it and the shop sells something people trust. But Daniel's teaching job could shrink badly by 2028, and by 2031 a fund with a fleet of robots can grow lambs and wheat cheaper than me. I think our income falls hard even if we keep the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd sit down with three neighbours and start a farmers' co-op to buy robots together, so we're not undercut alone. We'd build the savings to two years of costs and hold off the cold room. I'd lobby our MP for a law that stops investment funds buying farmland. And Daniel would start looking at school leadership or special needs teaching, where people still matter most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I'd say, but not frozen. I can see the shape of a plan, which helps. What scares me is how short two years is for a whole valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2028 and the robots about three years after. How does that split work out for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's almost a blessing, because the thinking part of my job is the bit I like least. The grants and the records go to AI in 2028 and I'm out with the sheep more. Then the robots come in 2031, and that's when I'd need the co-op in place, so those three years are my window to get organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off the cold room. What else gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The family holiday in Portugal we'd planned for next summer, and the new pickup. I'd keep the kids' riding lessons and Hana's extra science tutoring, because those are about their futures. Tomas's wage stays, that's not up for discussion.

say: I'd say the **land must stay** with the people who live on it.
I'd ask the government to decide **who gets the gains** before the companies do.
think: I think the farm survives, but **Daniel's teaching** income could shrink badly by 2028.
By 2031, **robot-run funds** could produce lamb and wheat cheaper than me.
do: Start a **farmers' co-op** with three neighbours this year to buy robots together.
Build savings to **two years** of costs and hold off the cold room.
Lobby the MP for a law stopping **investment funds** buying farmland.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to see the shape of a plan.
**Scared** by how short two years is for the whole valley.
S2.quote: The grants and the records go to AI in 2028 and I'm out with the sheep more.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year gap** as a window to organise neighbours before robots arrive.
The household's biggest risk is **Daniel's job**, not her own work.
She protects **Tomas's wage** and the kids' futures before her own comforts.

steps.text: Start a farmers' co-op with three neighbours to buy robots

Lobby the MP for a ban on funds buying farmland
Help Daniel look into special needs teaching roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like with the fast one, I'd say this is the time to get organised, and five years is enough if we start now. I'd write to the farming press about a public fund that helps small farms share robots. I'd say it calmly, because panicking helps nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years changes a lot for us. Daniel has time to move into a school role that's safer, and I have time to watch the first robots on other farms before I buy. I think we come through it, though the valley might look very different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the cold room plan this time, because the shop is the bit that machines can't copy easily. I'd join a pilot of robot weeders that the agricultural college runs, so I learn on someone else's kit. And I'd start the neighbours' co-op in about 2029, once we know which robots work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can live with. There's time to watch and learn before I bet the farm. That makes all the difference to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the shop is what machines can't copy easily. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people drive forty minutes to buy my lamb because they've met me and seen the ewes in the field. A robot farm can make cheaper meat, but it can't stand at the counter and tell you which field your Sunday roast grazed on. That trust took twelve years to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for Tomas in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Tomas get his own few hectares sooner, maybe renting him the top fields at a fair rate in 2030. If the robots come in 2034, he's better off owning a small place with a story behind it than being a hired shepherd. I'd hate to lose him, but I'd hate more for him to be stuck.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to get organised if we start now.
I'd write to the farming press backing a **public fund** for shared robots.
think: I think **Daniel** has time to move into a safer school role.
I can **watch the first robots** on other farms before I buy any.
do: Go ahead with the **cold room**, because the shop is hard for machines to copy.
Join the agricultural college's **robot weeder pilot** to learn on its kit.
Start the **neighbours' co-op** in about 2029, once proven robots exist.
feel: **Uneasy**, but in a way she can live with.
S3.quote: A robot farm can make cheaper meat, but it can't stand at the counter and tell you which field your Sunday roast grazed on.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her from **defensive** to **planning**.
She sees the **farm shop's trust** as her real protection against robot farms.
She would help **Tomas** get his own land rather than keep him dependent.

steps.text: Build the second cold room for the farm shop
Join the college's robot weeder pilot to learn the machines
Start the neighbours' robot co-op in about 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decade to make sure this works for farming families, not just the people who own the robots. I'd be pushing the farmers' union to write a plan now: shared machines, fair land rules, training for workers. I'd be one of the people at the front of that, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is a comfortable runway for us. I'll be 53 when the robots are good, Hana and Leo will be grown, and the mortgage will be nearly gone. I think we'll be fine, and my job is to help the valley be fine too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the normal things first: cold room, keep saving, keep the flock. Then from about 2030 I'd learn the planning tools properly and help set up the machinery co-op. And we'd tell Hana to stick with the vet plan, because animals that are ill still need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like weather you can see coming over the hill, and we've got a good roof. I'd worry for others more than for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is enough for Hana to qualify as a vet. Does that worry you, given robots by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, but I think a vet is one of the last jobs to go, because you're dealing with a frightened animal and an upset owner. I'd rather Hana do something she loves with her hands than chase whatever looks safe this year. Nobody knows what's safe in 2039, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change now, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd plant the new hedges and the orchard on the bottom field this winter. Whatever happens with robots, people will want to come and walk on a farm that looks after the land. That's the bit of Brook End I want the kids to inherit.

say: I'd say this decade must make it work for **farming families**, not just robot owners.
I'd push the **farmers' union** to write a plan for shared machines and land rules.
think: I think ten years is a **comfortable runway** for our family.
I'd be **53** when the robots arrive, with the mortgage nearly gone.
do: Keep the **flock and savings** going, and build the cold room.
Learn the **planning tools** properly from about 2030 and set up the co-op.
Plant **hedges and an orchard** on the bottom field this winter.
feel: **Calm**, more worried for others than for her own family.
S4.quote: Nobody knows what's safe in 2039, honestly.
fieldNote: With a decade she is **calm**, owning land with the mortgage almost paid.
She sees herself as a **leader** in the farmers' union on fair land and machine sharing.
She supports **Hana's vet plans**, valuing love of work over chasing safety.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because two years is too short for a whole valley to organise, and the funds would get there first. What would help is a law keeping farmland in the hands of people who farm it, and public money to help small farms share robots. I'd also want proper help for teachers like Daniel to move into new roles.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the land itself. Whatever the machines do, the soil and the hedges outlast all of us. I'd want someone to ask who'll look after them. That matters more to me than who drives the tractor.

headlineQuote: Whatever the machines do, the soil and the hedges outlast all of us.
